patterns.name: Complexity Analysis
patterns.explanation: Reasoning about the asymptotic time and space cost of an algorithm using Big-O, Omega, and Theta. Includes amortized analysis (the doubling trick for dynamic arrays) and the difference between worst-case, average-case, and expected-case complexity.
patterns.when_to_use: Always — before writing a single line of code on a hard problem. Constraints like `n <= 10^5` mean O(N log N) is the budget; `n <= 10^9` rules out anything touching every element. Use complexity analysis to *select* the algorithm, not to justify it after the fact.
patterns.intuition: Each operation has a cost; loops multiply costs; recursion sums them along the call tree. Drop constants and lower-order terms because at scale only the dominant factor matters. The point of Big-O is to predict whether your code will finish before the time limit — nothing more.
common_pitfalls: Treating O(N log N) and O(N) as 'basically the same' when N is large
Forgetting nested-loop multiplication when one of the loops is hidden inside a library call (e.g., `arr.includes` inside another loop)
Confusing space *used* with space *allocated* (e.g., recursion stack depth)
Ignoring the cost of string concatenation in a loop
patterns.complexity_signature: Predictive — answers 'will this fit in the time limit?'

patterns.name: Direct Simulation
patterns.explanation: Translate the problem statement literally into code: model the state, advance it step by step, and produce the answer. No clever insight — just a clean, correct mechanical execution of the rules.
patterns.when_to_use: When constraints are small (`n <= 10^4`), when the problem describes a process explicitly ('every second...', 'on each turn...'), or when the optimal algorithm is unknown but a brute simulation will fit. Also the right first step when prototyping before optimizing.
patterns.intuition: Most 'tricky' problems become trivial once you faithfully model the state. The hard part is identifying the *minimal* state that fully determines the next step, then advancing it without bugs.
common_pitfalls: Off-by-one in loop bounds when translating 1-indexed problem statements
Mutating shared state across simulation steps and corrupting later iterations
Re-reading input or recomputing invariants inside the inner loop
Missing a termination condition (infinite loop on a cycle)
patterns.complexity_signature: Usually O(N · steps) time, O(state-size) space

patterns.name: Integer Math & Modular Arithmetic
patterns.explanation: Working with integer division, remainder, GCD/LCM, and modular arithmetic — including modular exponentiation by repeated squaring and modular inverse via Fermat's little theorem (when the modulus is prime).
patterns.when_to_use: When the problem says 'return the answer modulo 10^9 + 7', when working with very large counts/products that would overflow, when computing combinations mod p, or when the structure is naturally periodic (clock arithmetic, calendar problems).
patterns.intuition: Modular arithmetic is just arithmetic on a circle of size M. Addition and multiplication are well-defined on the circle, but division requires the modular inverse. Fast exponentiation halves the exponent at each step, giving O(log E) multiplications.
common_pitfalls: Forgetting to take mod after every addition/multiplication and overflowing intermediate results
Using `/` for modular division instead of multiplying by the modular inverse
Negative numbers under `%` in C/Java/JS (use `((x % M) + M) % M`)
Computing `pow(a, b)` directly instead of by repeated squaring
patterns.complexity_signature: GCD: O(log min(a,b)). Modpow: O(log E). Sieve: O(N log log N).

patterns.name: Prefix & Running Aggregates
patterns.explanation: Maintain a running sum, product, max, min, or XOR while scanning. The aggregate at index `i` is computed in O(1) from the aggregate at `i-1`, enabling range queries in O(1) after O(N) preprocessing.
patterns.when_to_use: When a problem asks repeatedly about ranges of an array, when the answer at each index depends on everything before it, or when you would otherwise nest two loops to recompute the same partial answer.
patterns.intuition: If you've already computed `sum(0..i-1)`, you can get `sum(0..i)` for free. Range sums then become two prefix lookups. The same technique applies to any associative operation (max, XOR, count).
common_pitfalls: Confusing inclusive vs. exclusive prefix conventions and ending up with off-by-one bugs
Forgetting to handle the empty prefix (prefix[0] = identity element)
Using prefix max/min where it's not actually associative in the way you want
Not using a `prefix[]` array of size N+1 when you need range `[l, r)` queries

patterns.name: Sieve of Eratosthenes & Primes
patterns.explanation: Generate all primes up to N in O(N log log N) by sieving. Variants include the linear sieve, smallest-prime-factor sieve (for fast factorization), and segmented sieve for very large ranges.
patterns.when_to_use: When the problem asks about prime counts, divisors, or factorizations across a range up to ~10^7. Also when you need fast trial division by precomputing the smallest prime factor.
patterns.intuition: Mark every multiple of every prime starting from p². Each composite is marked O(log log N) times on average — once per distinct prime factor. The 'smallest-prime-factor' variant lets you factor any n ≤ N in O(log n) lookups.
common_pitfalls: Starting the inner loop at 2p instead of p² (correct but slower)
Using a `bool[]` larger than memory (the sieve is the bottleneck for N = 10^8+)
Forgetting that 1 is not prime
Re-running the sieve inside a query loop
patterns.complexity_signature: O(N log log N) time, O(N) space

patterns.name: Base Conversion & Bit Basics
patterns.explanation: Convert numbers between bases (2, 10, 16) and read their bit-level structure. Includes extracting digits via repeated `% base`, building from digits via `* base + d`, and the foundational bit operations (set/clear/test).
patterns.when_to_use: Whenever the problem treats a number as a string of digits or bits — palindrome numbers, digit sums, bit counts, balanced ternary, Gray codes. Also a prerequisite for the Bit Manipulation topic.
patterns.intuition: A number in base B is just a polynomial evaluated at B with coefficients 0..B-1. Multiplication by B shifts left; division by B with remainder peels the lowest digit.
common_pitfalls: Building digits in reverse order then forgetting to reverse them
Mishandling 0 as a special case (zero-digit number vs. one '0' digit)
Negative numbers and two's complement when reading bits
Off-by-one between 'highest set bit position' and 'number of bits'
